notes:
THIS BUILD HAD NO SCRIPTURE IN IT AT ALL. Seven beats, all white, and
the trial that decides the whole thing was summarized rather than heard. Mark 15
is a shouting match, and none of the shouting was in the video.

LIFTED VERBATIM AS SCRIPTURE (light blue -- Pilate is a man in the story and the
crowd is a crowd; neither is Deity and a red-letter KJV inks neither):
  s9   Mark 15:9   'Will ye that I release unto you the King of the Jews?'
       -- Pilate. n1a is trimmed to the frame and n1a2 carries the retelling.
  s13  Mark 15:13  'Crucify him.'  -- the crowd. n2 is trimmed to the frame and
       n2b carries the retelling.
  s14  Mark 15:14  'Why, what evil hath he done?'  -- Pilate again. This is the
       line the whole video needs and it was missing entirely: the man with the
       power to stop it saying out loud that there was no case. n2c retells it.

NO RED, DELIBERATELY. Jesus does speak in this trial -- Mark 15:2, 'Thou sayest
it,' answering Pilate, and a red-letter KJV inks it. It was left out. Two words
of ambiguous Old English dropped into the middle of a shouting match would need
paragraphs of explanation to land, and this video's spine is the swap, not the
interrogation. Left out on judgment, not uncertainty; the verse is exact if a
later pass wants it.

NO GREEN: the Father does not speak in Mark 15.

WOMEN: Mark 15:6-15 records no woman speaking. (Pilate's wife speaks in Matthew
27:19 -- 'Have thou nothing to do with that just man' -- but that is Matthew, not
this chapter, and this video is not about Pilate's conscience. Left out on
judgment.)

WHY-LAW: a guilty man walked out of the courtyard free because the innocent one
took the exact sentence he had earned. Milk: that is the whole gospel in one
swap, and Barabbas did nothing to deserve it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was the custom at Passover for the governor to release one prisoner the crowd chose. Pilate had two men: Jesus, and a killer named Barabbas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate could see Jesus had done nothing worth death. So he put the choice to the crowd himself.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Will ye that I release unto you the King of the Jews?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you want me to release the King of the Jews to you? He was almost offering it to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He thought the crowd would surely pick the innocent one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the chief priests worked the crowd, and they shouted for Barabbas instead. Pilate asked them what he should do with Jesus, then — and they answered with one word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Crucify him. That was it. That was the answer. And Pilate could not make sense of it.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Why, what evil hath he done?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Why? he asked them. What has he actually done? The man holding all the power in that courtyard said out loud that there was no case — and then handed him over anyway.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the guilty man walked free, and the innocent one was handed over in his place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Think about what Barabbas got: he was condemned, and then someone else took his exact sentence. He walked out free because Jesus took his cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That's not just Barabbas's story. That's the whole gospel in one swap — the innocent for the guilty, so the guilty could go free.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Barabbas walked free because the Son of God took his place. So can you. That's the whole point.

stills_wanted.ST2: ST2 now carries the frame, Pilate's verbatim question, and its retelling. Frame him putting it to them: Pilate at the front of the stone platform, half turned toward the crowd below, one hand open toward the two prisoners behind him. He is offering, not judging — he expects this to be easy.
stills_wanted.ST4: ST4 now carries five beats — the crowd's verbatim 'Crucify him,' Pilate's verbatim 'What evil hath he done?', and three retellings. Frame the collision, not the mob: the front rank of the crowd with mouths open mid-shout, and above them Pilate leaning out over the rail with his hands spread, arguing back at people who have stopped listening. Both sides in one shot, neither winning.
